```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
  fig.align = "center", fig.pos = "htbp", out.extra = ""
)

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(knitr)
  library(kableExtra)
  library(patchwork)
})

source(file.path("..", "R", "03-fit-models.R"))

processed <- readRDS(file.path("..", "data", "processed", "marathon.rds"))
all_finishers <- processed$all_finishers
run <- processed$analysis

primary <- fit_marathon_model(run)
coefs <- coef(primary)
b0 <- coefs[["(Intercept)"]]
b1 <- coefs[["half_min"]]
fit_summary <- summary(primary)
diag <- model_diagnostics(primary)

# HC1 standard errors and 95% confidence intervals for both coefficients.
estimates <- slope_interval(primary)
slope_ci <- estimates[estimates$term == "half_min", ]
# Distance of the slope from 2 in standard errors, and how many times larger
# the standard error would have to be for the 95% interval to reach 2.
ses_from_2 <- (b1 - 2) / slope_ci$std_error
se_factor <- ses_from_2 / qt(0.975, df.residual(primary))

n_analysis <- nrow(run)
n_finishers <- nrow(all_finishers)
n_dropped <- n_finishers - n_analysis

pct_positive <- 100 * mean(run$second_half_min > run$half_min)
median_ratio <- median(run$split_ratio)

# Minutes by which the doubling rule falls short of the fitted prediction at a
# given halfway split: (beta0 + beta1 * x) - 2x.
shortfall <- function(x) b0 + (b1 - 2) * x
median_split <- median(run$half_min)
shortfall_median <- shortfall(median_split)
# Halfway split at which the fitted line crosses the even-pacing line y = 2x.
split_crossing <- -b0 / (b1 - 2)
n_below_crossing <- sum(run$half_min < split_crossing)

# Residual spread and coverage of the usual prediction interval by decile.
deciles <- spread_by_decile(primary, run)
spread_ratio <- max(deciles$resid_sd) / min(deciles$resid_sd)
usual_pi <- predict(primary, newdata = data.frame(half_min = 105), interval = "prediction")
usual_width <- usual_pi[, "upr"] - usual_pi[, "lwr"]

# Prediction intervals built from runners within 5 minutes of each split.
pred_splits <- c(90, 105, 120, 135, 150)
local_pi <- bind_rows(lapply(pred_splits, function(x0) {
  local_prediction_interval(primary, run, x0)
}))
local_pi$width <- local_pi$upr - local_pi$lwr

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 10))
theme_update(
  panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
  plot.title = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold")
)

fmt <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits, big.mark = ",")
hms <- function(minutes) {
  total <- round(minutes * 60)
  sprintf("%d:%02d:%02d", total %/% 3600, (total %% 3600) %/% 60, total %% 60)
}
```

The code used to download, prepare, and analyze the data is available at
<https://github.com/pujithabobbili/simple-regression-project>.

# Abstract {.unnumbered}

Doubling a runner's halfway time is a common way to project a marathon finish,
but it assumes that the two halves take equal time. Using official results for
`r fmt(n_analysis, 0)` finishers of the 2023 Boston Marathon [@fay2023boston],
I fitted a simple linear regression of net finishing time on half-marathon
split, both in minutes, and compared the slope with 2, the value implied by
equal halves. The estimated slope was `r fmt(b1, 3)` (95% confidence interval
`r fmt(slope_ci$conf_low, 3)` to `r fmt(slope_ci$conf_high, 3)`), so each extra
minute at halfway is associated with about `r fmt(b1 - 1, 2)` extra minutes in
the second half. Doubling therefore underestimates the average finish by about
`r fmt(shortfall(90), 0)` minutes at a 1:30 split and about
`r fmt(shortfall(150), 0)` minutes at a 2:30 split. Because finishing times
also spread out more for slower runners, a 95% prediction interval for one
runner is about `r fmt(local_pi$width[1], 0)` minutes wide at a 1:30 split but
about `r fmt(local_pi$width[5], 0)` minutes wide at 2:30.

# Introduction

If a runner reaches the halfway point of a marathon in 1 hour 45 minutes,
doubling that time gives a projected finish of 3 hours 30 minutes. This
works exactly only when the runner completes the second half in another 1 hour
45 minutes. Any slowdown after halfway makes the projection too optimistic.

Running the second half more slowly than the first is called a positive split.
Previous studies have found that positive splits are common in marathons.
@march2011age and @santoslozano2014influence reported differences in pacing
across runners of different abilities, and March et al. found that slower and
less experienced runners tended to slow more. Earlier research also found that
men slowed more than women on average [@deaner2015men], that warmer conditions
were associated with larger slowdowns, especially among slower runners
[@ely2008effect], and that some recreational runners have severe late-race
slowdowns [@smyth2021how]. These studies compare groups of runners, but they do
not give one finishing-time equation that a runner could use at halfway.

In this paper, I ask two questions. First, how closely does the halfway split
predict net finishing time in the 2023 Boston Marathon? Second, how far does
the doubling rule miss, and for whom? If every runner kept an even pace,
finishing time would rise by exactly 2 minutes for each extra minute at
halfway. Because positive splits are common and slower runners tend to slow
more, I expect the slope to be above 2, so that doubling underestimates the
finish, and by more for slower runners. To check this, I fitted a simple linear
regression of net finishing time on half-marathon split for the
`r fmt(n_analysis, 0)` finishers with a recorded split.

The estimated slope is `r fmt(b1, 3)`, so the expectation holds: an extra
minute at halfway is associated with about `r fmt(b1, 2)` extra minutes at the
finish, including about `r fmt(b1 - 1, 2)` extra minutes in the second half.
The uncertainty of a projection for one runner also grows with the split, so
the halfway clock is less informative for slower runners. @sec-data describes
the data, @sec-methods explains the model and its checks, @sec-results presents
the results, and @sec-discussion discusses their limits and possible
extensions.

# Data {#sec-data}

## Source and observational units

I used the official results of the Boston Marathon held on April 17, 2023.
@fay2023boston compiled the file from results published by the
@baa2023results and made it available through the SCORE Network Sports Data
Repository. Each row represents one finisher. The full file has
`r fmt(n_finishers, 0)` finishers, so it covers the finishing field rather than
a random sample of it. Runners who started but did not finish are not
included. The times come from electronic timing chips, which record when a
runner crosses mats along the course; they do not show what happened between
the mats.

Since the complete finishing field is observed, the fitted line describes the
runners in this race directly. The confidence intervals require a broader
interpretation: I use them as model-based measures of uncertainty for similar
runners racing under similar conditions, rather than as uncertainty from
sampling the 2023 finishing field.
Boston also has a selective entry process: most entrants meet a qualifying-time
standard at an earlier marathon, and others enter through charity programs. Its
runners are therefore not a random sample of all marathon runners, which limits
how widely the results apply.

## Variables

The source file contains 15 columns with runner information, finishing places,
and race times. **Net finishing time**, the response, is the elapsed time
between crossing the starting mat and crossing the finishing mat, converted
from seconds to minutes. I used it rather than gun time, which starts at the
official signal and so also includes the wait to reach the start line: in this
file, gun time exceeds net time by a median of
`r fmt(median(all_finishers$gun_min - all_finishers$finish_min), 1)` minutes
and by as much as
`r fmt(max(all_finishers$gun_min - all_finishers$finish_min), 1)` minutes.
**Half-marathon split**, the explanatory variable, is the net elapsed time at
the halfway mat, also in minutes. From these two, I calculated the second-half
time (finishing time minus split) and the split ratio (second-half time divided
by split); a ratio above 1 means a slower second half. Sex
(`r fmt(100 * mean(run$sex == "Women"), 1)`% women) and age group (ten bands,
with `r fmt(100 * mean(run$age_group != "18-39"), 1)`% of finishers aged 40 or
over) are used only to describe the field.

The times are recorded to about one second, which is negligible next to the
`r fmt(sd(run$half_min), 1)`-minute standard deviation of halfway splits. A
more important point is that finishing time includes the halfway split, so a
strong association between the two is built in.

## Missing data and field characteristics {#sec-field}

There are `r n_dropped` finishers
(`r fmt(100 * n_dropped / n_finishers, 2)`% of the field) without a recorded
half-marathon split, probably because of a missed chip reading. I excluded
them, leaving `r fmt(n_analysis, 0)` runners. Their mean finishing time
(`r fmt(mean(all_finishers$finish_min[is.na(all_finishers$half_min)]), 1)`
minutes) is close to that of the runners retained
(`r fmt(mean(run$finish_min), 1)` minutes), and their sex and age-group make-up
is similar, so the exclusion is unlikely to matter. No other variable used here
has missing values, and there are no duplicate runners.

@tbl-summary summarizes the analysis variables, and @fig-distributions shows
their distributions. All three times have long upper tails. The median split
ratio is `r fmt(median_ratio, 3)`, so the typical finisher took about
`r fmt(100 * (median_ratio - 1), 1)`% longer for the second half, and
`r fmt(pct_positive, 1)`% of finishers ran a positive split. Pacing was similar
for women and men: both groups had a median split ratio of
`r fmt(median(run$split_ratio[run$sex == "Women"]), 3)`, even though women's
median finish (`r hms(median(run$finish_min[run$sex == "Women"]))`) was later
than men's (`r hms(median(run$finish_min[run$sex == "Men"]))`). All runners
also faced the same course on the same day, so this file cannot separate
weather from pacing; earlier work links heat to larger slowdowns, particularly
for slower runners [@ely2008effect].

```{r}
#| label: tbl-summary

All three times are right skewed, and the median split ratio of 1.058 means that the typical finisher ran the second half about 6% slower than the first."
describe_variable <- function(values, label, digits) {
  quartiles <- quantile(values, c(0.25, 0.75))
  data.frame(
    Variable = label,
    Mean = mean(values),
    SD = stats::sd(values),
    Min = min(values),
    Q1 = quartiles[[1]],
    Median = median(values),
    Q3 = quartiles[[2]],
    Max = max(values)
  ) %>%
    mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ formatC(.x, format = "f", digits = digits)))
}

summary_table <- bind_rows(
  describe_variable(run$half_min, "Half-marathon split", 1),
  describe_variable(run$finish_min, "Net finishing time", 1),
  describe_variable(run$second_half_min, "Second-half time", 1),
  describe_variable(run$split_ratio, "Split ratio", 3)
)

kable(
  summary_table, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
  align = c("l", rep("r", 7))
) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position"), font_size = 9)
```

## Additional and alternative data

Several additional data sources could help explain the pacing pattern. The
Boston Athletic Association publishes 5 km splits, which could show where a
runner began to slow. Results from other years and other marathons would allow
comparisons across courses and conditions. Hourly weather records from the
National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration could be matched to the period
when runners were on the course. Qualifying times would provide information
about recent performance before race day.

# Methods {#sec-methods}

## The model

For runner $i$, let $Y_i$ be net finishing time and $x_i$ be the half-marathon
split, both in minutes, for $i = 1, \dots, n$ with
$n = `r fmt(n_analysis, 0)`$. The simple linear regression model is
$$Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad
  \varepsilon_i \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2).$$
The intercept $\beta_0$ is the expected finishing time at a split of zero,
which is impossible in a race, so it only positions the line. The slope
$\beta_1$ is the expected difference in finishing time for a one-minute
difference in split. The error $\varepsilon_i$ is the difference between
runner $i$'s finishing time and the mean for runners with the same split; the
errors are assumed independent and normal with mean 0 and constant variance
$\sigma^2$. I estimated $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ by ordinary least squares,
which minimizes the sum of squared vertical distances
$\sum_{i=1}^{n} (Y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2$, and $\sigma$ by the residual
standard deviation $\hat\sigma$.

If both halves took the same time for every runner, then $Y_i = 2x_i$, which
corresponds to $\beta_0 = 0$ and $\beta_1 = 2$. A slope of 2 alone would not
establish equal pacing, because a nonzero intercept could still produce a
systematic difference between the halves, so I also compare the whole fitted
line with the doubling rule. A slope above 2 means that runners who reach
halfway later also lose more time in the second half. I
answer the second research question with the 95% confidence interval for
$\beta_1$, which shows how far the slope is from 2, and by comparing the fitted
line with the doubling rule at several splits. I used one predictor because the
question is about what can be estimated from the halfway clock alone, and I
kept both variables in minutes so that the slope can be compared directly
with 2.

For a runner with split $x_0$, the fitted finishing time is
$\hat{Y}_0 = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 x_0$. A confidence interval describes
the average finish of runners with that split, while a prediction interval
describes one runner and must also allow for that runner's own distance from
the line, so it is much wider.

## Assumptions and diagnostics

@fig-diagnostics shows the checks of the model assumptions.

**Linearity.** The residual plot shows no clear curve, so a straight line is a
reasonable summary of the average relationship over the observed range.

**Independence.** The model treats the errors of different runners as
unrelated. This is hard to justify fully in a race, because runners may follow
the same pacing group or respond similarly to course conditions. If so, the
data hold less independent information than `r fmt(n_analysis, 0)` runners
suggest, and even the robust standard error in @sec-validation would be too
small, making the slope's confidence interval too narrow. The slope estimate
itself would not be biased, and the conclusion would not change: the slope is
about `r fmt(ses_from_2, 0)` standard errors above 2, so its standard error
would have to be about `r fmt(se_factor, 0)` times larger before the interval
reached 2. The prediction intervals describe how far individual runners fall
from the line, which dependence between runners changes little.

**Constant variance.** This assumption does not hold. The band of residuals
widens as fitted times increase: the residual standard deviation rises from
`r fmt(min(deciles$resid_sd), 1)` minutes in the fastest tenth of the field to
`r fmt(max(deciles$resid_sd), 1)` minutes in the slowest, about a
`r fmt(spread_ratio, 1)`-fold increase. @sec-validation explains how I
handle this.

**Normality.** The histogram of residuals is centered near zero but right
skewed, with a long upper tail of runners who finished much later than
predicted. With this many runners, the confidence interval for the slope is
still reliable, but a prediction interval that relies on normal errors is not.

I also examined Cook's distance, which measures how much the fitted line would
move if one runner were removed. The largest value is
`r fmt(diag$max_cooks, 3)`, well below the usual reference value of 1, so no
single runner drives the fit. I kept runners with unusual pacing because they
are real race results.

```{r}
#| label: fig-diagnostics
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 3.9
#| fig-cap: "Regression diagnostics. Top left: residuals against fitted values show no clear curve but widen as fitted times increase. Top right: the histogram of residuals is centered near zero but right skewed, with a long upper tail; its horizontal axis is limited to $-60$ to 90 minutes. Bottom: the residual standard deviation within each tenth of the halfway split rises from about 6 to 14 minutes, so the constant-variance assumption does not hold."
aug <- diag$augmented

d1 <- ggplot(aug, aes(fitted, resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.05, size = 0.3, colour = "grey25") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#B2182B", linewidth = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Fitted finishing time (min)", y = "Residual (min)",
       title = "Residuals vs fitted")

d2 <- ggplot(aug, aes(resid)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "grey35", colour = NA) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#B2182B", linewidth = 0.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-60, 90)) +
  labs(x = "Residual (min)", y = "Runners",
       title = "Histogram of residuals")

d3 <- ggplot(deciles, aes(mean_split, resid_sd)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2166AC", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(colour = "#2166AC", size = 1.6) +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(
    x = "Mean half-marathon split within each tenth of the field (min)",
    y = "Residual SD (min)",
    title = "Residual spread across the field"
  )

(d1 + d2) / d3
```

## Model selection and validation {#sec-validation}

I kept the model in its simplest form. Both variables stay in minutes, so the
slope can be compared directly with 2, and the residual plot shows no clear
curve, so a quadratic term was not needed. The failure of constant variance
has two consequences. First, the usual
standard errors assume one common variance. I therefore computed the standard
errors and confidence intervals with a heteroskedasticity-consistent (HC1)
estimator [@zeileis2004sandwich], which lets each runner's residual contribute
its own variance. This changes the intervals but not the fitted line.

Second, the usual prediction interval uses the single value $\hat\sigma$ for
every runner, so it has nearly the same width at every split. To see whether
that is a problem, I counted how often the usual 95% prediction interval
contains the actual finishing time within each tenth of the field. It contains
`r fmt(deciles$coverage[1], 1)`% of the fastest tenth but only
`r fmt(deciles$coverage[10], 1)`% of the slowest, so it is too wide for fast
runners and too narrow for slow ones. I therefore built prediction intervals
from nearby runners instead. For a split $x_0$, I took the runners whose splits
lie within 5 minutes of $x_0$ and added the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of
their residuals to $\hat{Y}_0$. These intervals widen where the spread is
larger and can be longer on the slow side, which matches the right skew of the
residuals. They leave out the uncertainty in the fitted line itself, which is
well under a minute at these splits and small next to the spread of runners.

## Possible extensions to the model

Adding sex and age group, with interactions with the split, would let the slope
differ between groups. Because women and men had similar split ratios, this
would probably change the slope little, and it would need more information than
the halfway clock provides. A quadratic term would let the line bend, but the
residual plot shows no clear curvature. Weighted least squares or quantile
regression would model the changing spread directly and could replace the
nearby-runner intervals with a single model.

## Software

The analysis was carried out in R version
`r paste(R.version$major, R.version$minor, sep = ".")` [@rcore2024]. I used
`dplyr` for data handling [@wickham2023dplyr] and `readr` to read the data
[@wickham2024readr]. Figures were made with `ggplot2` [@wickham2016ggplot2] and
combined using `patchwork` [@pedersen2024patchwork]. Robust standard errors came
from `sandwich` [@zeileis2004sandwich; @zeileis2020sandwich]. The report used
Quarto [@allaire2022quarto], `knitr` [@xie2023knitr], and `kableExtra`
[@zhu2024kableextra]. The regression was fitted with `lm` in R's `stats`
package.

# Results {#sec-results}

## The fitted model

The fitted line, with coefficients rounded for display, is
$$\widehat{\text{finish}} = `r fmt(b0, 2)` + `r fmt(b1, 3)` \times
  \text{half-marathon split}.$$
Both times are in minutes, and @tbl-coefs gives the estimates.

```{=latex}
\needlines{11}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-coefs
#| tbl-cap: "Least squares estimates for net finishing time regressed on halfway split, with heteroskedasticity-consistent (HC1) standard errors and 95% confidence intervals. The slope's interval, 2.210 to 2.225, lies entirely above 2, the value implied by equal halves."
coef_table <- estimates %>%
  transmute(
    Term = c("Intercept", "Half-marathon split"),
    Estimate = formatC(estimate, format = "f", digits = 3),
    `Std. error (HC1)` = formatC(std_error, format = "fg", digits = 3, flag = "#"),
    `95% CI` = paste(
      formatC(conf_low, format = "f", digits = 3), "to",
      formatC(conf_high, format = "f", digits = 3)
    )
  )

kable(
  coef_table, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r")
) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position"), font_size = 9)
```

The slope's 95% confidence interval,
`r fmt(slope_ci$conf_low, 3)`--`r fmt(slope_ci$conf_high, 3)`, lies entirely
above 2, so the fitted relationship is steeper than the doubling rule. For
runners whose splits differ by one minute, the model estimates a difference of
about `r fmt(b1, 2)` minutes at the finish, about `r fmt(b1 - 1, 2)` minutes of
which comes in the second half. The negative intercept has no race meaning,
since a zero-minute split is far outside the observed range of
`r fmt(min(run$half_min), 1)`--`r fmt(max(run$half_min), 1)` minutes. The model
has $R^2 = `r fmt(fit_summary$r.squared, 3)`$, but much of this comes from
finishing time containing the split, so the residual standard deviation of
`r fmt(fit_summary$sigma, 2)` minutes is a more useful measure of fit.

@fig-scatter shows the fitted line with the doubling rule. The two lines cross
at a split of about `r hms(split_crossing)`; only `r n_below_crossing` runners
were faster than that. For everyone else, the model predicts a later finish
than doubling, and the gap grows with the split.

```{r}
#| label: fig-scatter
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-cap: 'Net finishing time against halfway split for 26,526 finishers, with the fitted regression line (solid) and the doubling rule, $\text{finish} = 2 \times \text{split}$ (dashed). Darker areas hold more runners. The lines cross near a 1:07 split; above that, the fitted line lies above the doubling line, and the gap grows for slower runners.'
ggplot(run, aes(half_min, finish_min)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.05, size = 0.35, colour = "grey25") +
  geom_abline(
    aes(slope = 2, intercept = 0, linetype = "Doubling rule (y = 2x)"),
    colour = "#B2182B", linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_abline(
    aes(slope = b1, intercept = b0, linetype = "Fitted regression"),
    colour = "#2166AC", linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c("Doubling rule (y = 2x)" = "dashed", "Fitted regression" = "solid"),
    name = NULL,
    guide = guide_legend(override.aes = list(
      colour = c("#B2182B", "#2166AC"), linewidth = 0.7
    ))
  ) +
  labs(x = "Half-marathon split (minutes)", y = "Net finishing time (minutes)") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## What the model means for a runner

@tbl-predictions gives projected finishing times for five halfway splits. At a
1:30 split, the model adds about `r fmt(shortfall(90), 0)` minutes to the
doubled split; at 2:30, it adds about `r fmt(shortfall(150), 0)` minutes. For
the median split of `r hms(median_split)`, the difference is about
`r fmt(shortfall_median, 0)` minutes. A rough mental version is to double the
split and add one minute for every five minutes beyond 1:07, since
$\widehat{\text{finish}} - 2x = `r fmt(b0, 2)` + `r fmt(b1 - 2, 3)`x$.

```{=latex}
\needlines{15}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-predictions
#| tbl-cap: "Finishing-time projections for five halfway splits. 'Doubling short by' is the model projection minus the doubled split. Each 95% prediction interval adds the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the residuals of runners within 5 minutes of that split to the model projection, so it widens for slower splits and is longer on the slow side."
pred_table <- data.frame(
  Halfway = vapply(local_pi$half_min, hms, character(1)),
  Doubling = vapply(2 * local_pi$half_min, hms, character(1)),
  Model = vapply(local_pi$fit, hms, character(1)),
  `Doubling short by` = paste0(formatC(local_pi$fit - 2 * local_pi$half_min, format = "f", digits = 1), " min"),
  `95% prediction interval` = paste0(
    vapply(local_pi$lwr, hms, character(1)), " to ",
    vapply(local_pi$upr, hms, character(1))
  ),
  Width = paste0(formatC(local_pi$width, format = "f", digits = 0), " min"),
  check.names = FALSE
)

kable(
  pred_table, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
  align = c("l", "l", "l", "r", "l", "r")
) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position"), font_size = 9)
```

The prediction intervals show how uncertain a projection is for one runner.
They are about `r fmt(local_pi$width[1], 0)` minutes wide at a 1:30 split and
about `r fmt(local_pi$width[5], 0)` minutes wide at 2:30, compared with about
`r fmt(usual_width, 0)` minutes at every split for the usual interval. They are
also uneven: at a 1:45 split, a runner may finish up to about
`r fmt(local_pi$fit[2] - local_pi$lwr[2], 0)` minutes faster than projected but
up to about `r fmt(local_pi$upr[2] - local_pi$fit[2], 0)` minutes slower,
because some runners slow down sharply in the second half.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

For the 2023 Boston finishers, the halfway split predicts the finish closely,
but not in the way the doubling rule assumes. The fitted slope is
`r fmt(b1, 3)`, and its confidence interval lies above 2, as expected from how
common positive splits are: `r fmt(pct_positive, 0)`% of runners ran a slower
second half. Doubling therefore underestimates the average finish by about
`r fmt(shortfall(90), 0)` minutes for a 1:30 split and about
`r fmt(shortfall(150), 0)` minutes for a 2:30 split. This agrees with earlier
findings that slower runners slow more [@march2011age;
@santoslozano2014influence], and it summarizes the pattern in one equation that
a runner can use at halfway.

The average finish is estimated very precisely, but one runner's finish is not.
The 95% prediction interval is about `r fmt(local_pi$width[1], 0)` minutes wide
for a 1:30 split and about `r fmt(local_pi$width[5], 0)` minutes wide for a 2:30
split, so a projection should be read as an estimate of the mean, with more
uncertainty for slower runners.

The study has several limitations. The data include finishers only, so runners
who dropped out, possibly after slowing sharply, are missing, and the results
do not describe all starters. Boston's field is selective and raced one course
on one day, so a different race could produce a different slope. Runners who
race together may have related errors, which the model ignores. The
nearby-runner intervals are built and checked on the same data, so they should
be tested on another race before being used as forecasts. Finally, the model is
descriptive: it does not show that starting faster would make a runner finish
sooner.

Several extensions would be useful. The organizers' 5 km splits would show
where the slowdown begins, which relates to the late-race collapse studied by
@smyth2021how. Fitting several years with weather data would show whether the
slope changes with temperature [@ely2008effect], and adding sex and age group
could test the differences between groups reported by @deaner2015men.
